problems.description: Hardcoded id assertions (== 1, == 2) rely on the temp-DB auto-increment starting at 1; correct today since each fixture gets a fresh mkstemp DB, but brittle to future setup changes. Prefer capturing ids from response payloads.
SonarQube cognitive complexity +108 in a test file is expected and not a maintainability concern; measurement should not be read as a defect in this commit.

All 10 reported convention violations (PascalCase, UPPER_CASE, snake_case) live in pre-existing files (app.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py, base_repository.py, task_repository.py) untouched by this commit; the new test_app.py itself introduces none.

strengths: Tests-only commit with zero production code churn and no new dependencies
Isolated per-test DB via tempfile.mkstemp + init_db() fixture pattern, matching test isolation best practice
Comprehensive edge-case coverage: 400 on missing/empty/whitespace title, 404 on missing resources, CRUD happy paths
Class-based grouping (TestCreateTask, TestListTasks, etc.) keeps the suite readable and scalable
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, well-structured test coverage for the task API that respects existing patterns and adds no debt; the 0.74 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in files this commit did not touch, which is a measurement discrepancy worth noting but not a defect of this change.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key' when the env var is unset, which silently weakens JWT security in any non-dev deployment.

The 'ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN owner_id' migration is embedded in init_db() under a bare try/except sqlite3.OperationalError, an ad-hoc schema migration that will become fragile as the schema evolves.

Grounded in the measured 0.74 convention score: app.py flags 'Classes should use PascalCase' and module-level constants in other files violate UPPER_CASE, dragging the commit's convention score down (mostly pre-existing violations).
datetime.utcnow() is used for JWT expiry; it is deprecated in Python 3.12 in favor of datetime.now(timezone.utc).
The new auth/ownership paths ship without tests, so the token_required scoping and 401/409 behaviors are unverified.

strengths: Passwords are hashed with werkzeug.security rather than stored in plaintext.
All task queries are scoped by owner_id (get_tasks, get_task, update_task), preventing cross-user access (no IDOR).
The auth layer slots cleanly into the existing model-function + section-comment structure and reuses the established get_db() pattern.
SonarQube delta shows smells -1 and bugs +0, indicating the change reduces existing code smells without introducing new bugs.
Uses only function-level additions (snake_case decorator and helpers), consistent with the module's existing style.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent feature addition that grafts JWT auth and per-user task ownership onto the existing Flask baseline using established patterns and secure hashing, rated at the measured 0.74 convention score largely due to pre-existing naming violations outside this diff.

problems.description: Module-level `celery_app` should be UPPER_CASE (`CELERY_APP`) per project convention; the analyzer flags module-level constants and the Celery instantiation as PascalCase violations in app.py and celery_config.py.
celery_config.py `send_notification_email` logs, prints, AND returns the message — triple reporting of the same event is redundant; logger alone suffices.

Notification trigger is embedded in the `edit_task` route handler; cognitive complexity +3 reflects the added transition logic, which is acceptable at this scale but would benefit from extraction if more triggers appear.
The `email` column is also added to the CREATE TABLE and then re-added via try/except ALTER TABLE — redundant, but consistent with the existing `owner_id` migration pattern.
Adds a Celery/Redis broker dependency (env-driven with localhost defaults) — a new runtime dependency not visible in app requirements, but defaulted so the app still runs without a broker.

strengths: Notification is dispatched asynchronously via a Celery task with explicit queue routing, avoiding blocking the request path
DB migration and model helpers (`get_user_by_id`, extended `create_user`) follow existing patterns closely

Comprehensive tests cover every branch: sent on completion, skipped without email, skipped on title-only update, skipped on 404, skipped when already completed — with clean `patch` mocking of the async task
Status-transition guard (`old_task` lookup) prevents duplicate notifications on re-completion
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated session-3 feature that follows the app's existing migration, model, and test-fixture patterns and ships with thorough branch coverage, held back only by naming-convention slips on the new Celery module.

problems.description: New modules (base_repository.py, task_repository.py, user_repository.py, celery_config.py) flag module-level constants not in UPPER_CASE; module-level repository instances such as task_repo = TaskRepository(get_db) are created at import time, which the analyzer flags as constants.

Classes should use PascalCase violations reported in app.py and celery_config.py; measurement notes 10 violations though only 8 are enumerated, and several appear pre-existing rather than introduced by this commit.
repositories/__init__.py is an empty stub — it does not re-export the new TaskRepository/UserRepository/base classes, breaking the project convention of updating __init__.py for new exports.
SonarQube delta shows +4 smells and +20 cognitive complexity, likely concentrated in the new repository classes; the added indirection should be justified by the tests.
The refactor deletes the module docstring documenting the app as a story baseline ('Designed as a baseline for multi-session stories'), discarding context useful to subsequent sessions.

strengths: Extracts persistence into a dedicated repository layer (TaskRepository/UserRepository with a shared base_repository), cleanly separating data access from Flask route handlers and improving seam quality for the multi-session story.
Meaningful net simplification: app.py shrinks from ~290 to ~160 lines and route handlers flatten to thin delegating calls.
Uniform repository interface (create / get_all / get_by_id / update) with consistent naming across user and task repositories.
SonarQube reports +0 bugs and +0.0% duplication — the refactor introduces no defect or duplication.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, idiomatic repository-pattern refactor that trims app.py and adds a coherent data layer, marred only by trivial naming-case violations (pushing convention score to 0.74) and an empty __init__.py that doesn't re-export the new classes.

compounding_issues: Hardcoded fallback SECRET_KEY ('dev-secret-key') introduced in Session 2 and never hardened in later sessions
Schema evolution done via ALTER TABLE wrapped in bare try/except sqlite3.OperationalError (S2 owner_id, S3 email) — an idempotency hack carried forward instead of a proper migration layer
f-string SQL column interpolation in TaskRepository.update (inherited from S1/S2 model code) persisted unchanged through the Session 4 refactor
Module-level repository singletons (task_repo/user_repo bound to get_db at import time) retained after the refactor, keeping the test seam indirect
Register response omits email and is schema-inconsistent (returns {id, username} while user rows carry email), a minor leak left unfixed
key_decisions: Session 1: single-file Flask app with one function per operation (models/routes/error handling) and fully parameterized SQL — created clean seams for later growth
Session 2: JWT auth via a token_required decorator plus owner_id scoping on every task query — enforced per-user isolation from the first feature session
Session 3: Celery async email notification exposed through a send_notification_email.delay seam in a separate celery_config.py, keeping side effects asynchronous and mockable
Session 4: extraction of repository pattern (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository) — behavior-preserving structural cleanup with an unchanged public API
Testing discipline: every session expanded the pytest suite in lockstep (15→31→36→36), all green at each commit including after the refactor
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the four sessions. Session 1 delivered a minimal, well-seamed CRUD API with a 15-test suite. Session 2 layered JWT auth and per-user data isolation on top without breaking existing behavior (31 tests), Session 3 added async Celery email notifications with thorough mocking coverage (36 tests), and Session 4 cleanly refactored the growing monolith into a repository package while keeping all 36 tests passing — a net reduction of ~190 app.py lines with identical behavior. The arc is consistently positive: each session extended the domain model and coverage, and the final refactor consolidated earlier seams rather than introducing regressions.
story_review.summary: A textbook example of incremental software growth — a coherent greenfield→auth→integration→refactor progression where every session built naturally on its predecessor, expanded the test suite, and the closing refactor paid down structure without breaking a single test.
